headline: Halfway Rock groundfish steady, mackerel schools pull bass to the ledges
subhead: Two days off the new moon, the tide swing is doing exactly what a strong flood should do — stacking bait tight against structure from Peaks Island to Cape Small.
body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning drifting the eastern face of Halfway Rock with a spinning rod I have no business fishing off a boat, and it reminded me why I keep coming back to that piece of ledge every August. The rock sits where it always sits — six miles off Bailey Island, the same slab of granite it's been since before anyone I know was born — but what's happening around it changes by the week, and this week the change is worth writing down.

We're two days past the new moon, and the tidal flow it kicked up has done what building flow into a new moon usually does this time of year: sharpened the bite at the current-driven structure. I flagged that pattern building last week, and out at Halfway Rock it's arrived right on schedule. On the last two hours of the ebb, with the current really moving off the southeast corner, I marked pollock and cod stacked in that 60 to 90 foot depth where the ledge drops off into the channel. Diamond jigs — the heavier 4 to 6 ounce Norwegian-style jigs, worked with a short hop off bottom — took three keeper-class cod and a pile of pollock in about ninety minutes of fishing. Haddock have been scarcer out there than I'd like this month; I took one respectable fish and lost what felt like a bigger one on the way up, but the ratio of pollock to haddock this summer has been lopsided in pollock's favor. If you're going out for haddock specifically, fish the slack itself, right at the top of the tide, when the bait settles and they'll hold tighter to bottom rather than getting pushed off the structure by current.

The more interesting story this week, though, is what's happening in the upper water column. Mackerel schools have been thick and dependable through the bay all summer, and they haven't thinned yet — I've watched them roll on the surface off Spring Point, off the eastern side of Peaks Island, and in tight around the ledges off Cushing. That's the forage base holding this whole fishery together right now. Water's sitting in that classic Maine summer range, low 60s, which keeps mackerel comfortable and keeps striped bass working the edges where those schools get pinned against structure. Jigging small diamond jigs or Sabiki rigs off Peaks in 20 to 40 feet on the last of the incoming has been about as reliable as fishing gets in this bay — you can fill a five-gallon bucket in twenty minutes if the school is under the boat, and that bucket buys you the best live bait in Casco Bay for the bass.

Striped bass have been following that bait with the kind of patience I appreciate in a fish. River mouths — the Presumpscot, the mouth of the Royal, the Basin down toward Cape Small — have all been holding fish on the top of the tide and through the first two hours of the ebb, when baitfish get flushed out and bass set up to intercept them. Live mackerel under a slip float, fished right along the current seam where the river water meets the bay, has been the most consistent producer. For guys who'd rather cast than soak bait, a white or chartreuse bucktail worked slow along the bottom edge of those seams has taken slot fish as well, though I'd call that bite good, not great — you need to find the seam, not just the general area.

The ledge fishing for bass off Bailey Island and out toward Cape Small has been more of a dawn-and-dusk affair. I worked the ledges off Cape Small at first light Thursday with a topwater popper — a Yo-Zuri Sashimi, walked slow across the slick — and connected with two fish in the mid-20-inch range before the sun got high and the bite shut off. That's typical August ledge behavior here: the bass are there, but the window is short, tied tight to low light and moving water, and once the sun climbs and the tide slacks, they drop back into deeper water and go quiet. Two Lights has fished similarly — good for an hour around first light on a dropping tide, then it goes flat.

Bluefish remain the wildcard. There's a real push of bluefish moving up the coast right now, riding peanut bunker schools from the Sound clear up through Massachusetts Bay, and it wouldn't surprise me if some of that push works its way into outer Casco Bay before the month is out — we've had years where a late-August bluefish run shows up off Two Lights or out past Cushing almost overnight. I haven't seen it materialize inside the bay yet this week, and I'm not going to promise it's coming, but if you're rigging up for bass anyway, it costs nothing to keep a wire leader in the boat.

Looking ahead, I don't expect the broad pattern to shift much through the coming week. Water temperatures should hold steady in that low-60s range, mackerel should keep schooling reliably enough to bait up on, and the tidal flow — still building off this new moon cycle — should keep sharpening the bite at current-driven structure like Halfway Rock and the river mouths. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be back at Halfway Rock on the last two hours of an ebb tide with jigs in hand, and I'd have a bucket of fresh mackerel rigged for bass on the way home.
